solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Seducer reluctant to have a port

blocks.note: loth (or loath) means unwilling
taken as written
Rio de Janeiro, the Brazilian port

explanation.surface: A womaniser who would rather not drink a glass of port.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Port' reads as the drink, but it is a harbour city, here Rio. Lothario is the rake in Rowe's play The Fair Penitent.
explanation.definitionFit: The name of a stage rake became a common noun for any man who habitually seduces women.

clue.text: Small expanse of water Belloc handled, partly

indicators.note: only part of the following words is used, so the letters sit inside them

blocks.note: the run of letters spanning the two words

explanation.surface: The writer Hilaire Belloc dealt with a little patch of water, to some extent.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer straddles the end of the writer's surname and the start of the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: A lochan is the Scottish diminutive of loch, meaning a little lake or pool.

clue.text: Male keyboard player releasing current for one in kitchen

indicators.note: to release something is to let it go, so a letter is dropped

blocks.note: a man's name
someone who plays the piano
I is the symbol for electric current

explanation.surface: A man at the piano gives up electricity in exchange for a job in the kitchen.
explanation.walkthrough: TIM plus PIANIST without its first I. 'Kitchen' is orchestral slang for the percussion section, so it is no cook.
explanation.definitionFit: The kettledrum player sits among the percussion, which musicians jokingly call the kitchen because of its pots and pans.

clue.text: A brother helped, we’re told (scraped away!)

indicators.note: being told something means hearing it, so the word is taken by its sound

blocks.note: taken as written
BR is the standard abbreviation for brother
to aid is to help; the spelling is altered to match the sound

explanation.surface: Someone reports that a brother lent a hand, with a parenthetical shout about scraping.
explanation.walkthrough: A + BR then a word sounding like AIDED: said together they give 'a-BRAY-ded'.
explanation.definitionFit: To abrade is to wear down by rubbing or friction, so the past form matches worn off by grinding.

clue.text: Rise of number one team, one bound to be permanently revolutionary

definitions.text: one bound to be permanently revolutionary

indicators.note: in a down clue a rise reads from the bottom upward, turning the letters round

blocks.note: NO is the abbreviation for number, I is Roman one, and XI is a side of eleven players

explanation.surface: A top team climbs the table, with one of its members destined to be a revolutionary for ever.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Revolutionary' suggests politics, but it means spinning: Zeus bound Ixion to a fiery wheel that turns eternally.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth Ixion was punished by being tied to a burning wheel spinning through eternity, so he revolves endlessly.

clue.text: A bishop caught with horse outside church office

indicators.note: something outside wraps around what it is placed beyond

blocks.note: taken as written
B is the chess notation for bishop
a bay is a reddish-brown horse
C is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for caught

explanation.surface: A bishop is arrested on horseback just outside a church.
explanation.walkthrough: A + B, then BAY wrapped round C. 'Church office' looks like a building but means a post held.
explanation.definitionFit: An abbacy is the position, jurisdiction or term held by an abbot, an ecclesiastical post.

clue.text: Graduate nurse once, one keeping judge’s dog

indicators.note: to keep something is to hold it inside

blocks.note: Bachelor of Arts
State Enrolled Nurse, a former British nursing grade
Roman numeral one
J is the abbreviation for judge; the possessive just links it to the definition

explanation.surface: A graduate who used to nurse is looking after a judge's pet dog.
explanation.walkthrough: BA + SEN, then I holding J. SEN, a State Enrolled Nurse, was a British nursing qualification phased out in the 1990s.
explanation.definitionFit: The basenji is a small African hunting breed known for not barking, so it is a kind of canine.

clue.text: Friend has a turn crossing major road

indicators.note: something crossing another lies across it, here straddling it on both sides

blocks.note: taken as written
the M1, Britain's main north-south motorway
a go is a turn in a game

explanation.surface: A friend takes a turn while crossing a busy road.
explanation.walkthrough: The M1 is Britain's main motorway from London to Leeds; crosswords write its digit as the letter I.
explanation.definitionFit: Amigo is the Spanish word for a pal, widely borrowed into English for a mate or companion.

clue.text: Surrendering crop in conclusion of farming

indicators.note: the conclusion of a word is its final letter

blocks.note: the yield is the harvest produced
taken as written
the last letter of farming

explanation.surface: Giving up the harvest at the end of the farming year.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' is not a link here; it supplies its own two letters between the crop and the final letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To yield is to give way or submit, so the participle means giving up or capitulating.

clue.text: Gloomy signal from one who knows the score?

definitions.text: signal from one who knows the score

blocks.note: first meaning: pessimistic, depressed

blocks.clueFragment: signal from one who knows the score
blocks.note: second meaning: the conductor's downward stroke marking the first beat of a bar

explanation.walkthrough: 'Knows the score' sounds like being well informed, but the score is the written music and the one who knows it is the conductor.
explanation.definitionFit: Downbeat means pessimistic or low in mood, and is also the conductor's baton stroke that starts each bar.

clue.text: Cameroon is in her travels, whatever the circumstances

indicators.note: things that travel move about, so the letters are moved into a new order

blocks.note: fifteen letters taken as written

explanation.surface: A woman visits the African country of Cameroon on her journeys, no matter what.
explanation.walkthrough: The country is not geography here; it supplies letters, and 'her travels' only tells you to rearrange them.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means regardless of weather or conditions, so it covers any situation at all.

clue.text: Stop supporting a group with no backing

indicators.note: going backwards means reading the letters from right to left

blocks.note: taken as written
a band is a group of people or musicians
taken as written

explanation.surface: Withdrawing support from a group that has no one behind it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'With no backing' reads as 'unsupported', but the word NO is simply turned round.
explanation.definitionFit: To abandon someone is to desert them and cease giving them help or loyalty.

clue.text: Name a French poet’s sister’s calling

blocks.note: N is the abbreviation for name
un is French for a
Thomas Hood, nineteenth-century English poet

explanation.surface: Naming the career chosen by the sister of a French poet.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's of poet's belongs to the surface; the definition then needs its own possessive for 'sister'.
explanation.definitionFit: A sister is a nun, and her vocation is the religious life of the convent.

clue.text: Where a flyer may go for a walk in London

definitions.note: the answer is the first word of the street name Birdcage Walk

blocks.note: first meaning: a home for a pet bird
second meaning: the first word of the name of a road beside St James's Park in Westminster

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests an aviator taking a stroll; the flyer is a bird and the walk is a London street.
explanation.definitionFit: A cage for birds holds a canary or budgie, and Birdcage Walk is named after James I's royal aviaries there.

clue.text: Fervour of Republican entering in civic style?

indicators.note: something entering goes inside

blocks.note: R is the abbreviation for Republican
'à la' means in the style of, so 'à la city' is in the manner of a city

explanation.surface: The zeal of a Republican going into local politics in a civic-minded way.
explanation.walkthrough: R goes into A LA CITY. The question mark flags the playful reading of 'civic style' as French à la plus city.
explanation.definitionFit: Alacrity is eager readiness or brisk enthusiasm, close to fervour or keenness.

clue.text: American industrial leader, old and pale of face

indicators.note: the leader of a word is the letter at its front

blocks.note: the first letter of industrial
O is the abbreviation for old
wan means pallid

explanation.surface: An aging, ashen-faced US captain of industry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Industrial leader' looks like a tycoon, but it only gives the first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone from the Midwestern state of Iowa is a particular kind of US citizen.

clue.text: Females endlessly grabbing attention is fatiguing

indicators.note: without an end, so the final letter is cut off
to grab is to seize and hold within one's grasp

blocks.note: women are females
to give someone your ear is to pay attention
taken as written

explanation.surface: Women forever demanding attention is tiring.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Is' looks like the link before the definition but is part of the wordplay, tucked inside the shortened females.
explanation.definitionFit: Something wearisome is tedious and exhausting, which is what fatiguing means.

clue.text: This chap is a Pacific country’s star

blocks.note: 'he's' is short for 'he is'
Peru borders the Pacific, with the possessive 's kept

explanation.surface: A man described as the leading celebrity of a nation on the Pacific.
explanation.walkthrough: Both apostrophe-s endings are kept as plain S letters: HE'S + PERU'S.
explanation.definitionFit: Hesperus is the classical name for the evening star, the planet Venus seen after sunset.

clue.text: Additional passage from book court rejected

indicators.note: something rejected is thrown out, so those letters are removed

blocks.note: an extract is an excerpt from a text
CT is the abbreviation for court

explanation.surface: A further excerpt from a book that a court refused to admit as evidence.
explanation.walkthrough: EXTRACT minus CT. 'Additional passage' wants to be the definition, but 'passage' is needed for the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Extra as an adjective means more than usual or supplementary, the same as additional.

clue.text: A sign erected over Tyneside plant

indicators.note: putting upright in a down clue lifts the letters so they read from the bottom

blocks.note: taken as written
an omen is a portent
Tyneside, around Newcastle, is in the North East of England

explanation.surface: A signpost put up above a factory in Newcastle.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'over' means placed above, so the upturned sign comes before NE. 'Plant' wants to be a factory; it is a flower.
explanation.definitionFit: The anemone, or windflower, is a flowering species of the buttercup family.

clue.text: A right pain around Ealing at first, like the bloody Tube!

indicators.note: what comes first in a word is its opening letter
to go around something is to surround it

blocks.note: taken as written
R is the abbreviation for right
a trial is a nuisance or ordeal
the first letter of Ealing, a west London district

explanation.surface: A grumble about the London Underground: going via Ealing is a real nuisance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A right pain' reads as one idiom, but splits into A, R and TRIAL. The Tube is not the Underground but a blood vessel, hence 'bloody' (which in British slang is also a mild swear).
explanation.definitionFit: An artery is a tube carrying blood from the heart, so arterial describes such a blood-filled vessel.

clue.text: Put out again about subject under discussion

blocks.note: re means concerning
the issue is the matter being debated

explanation.surface: Publishing something a second time on the topic currently being debated.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' looks like a container signal but here is simply RE.
explanation.definitionFit: To reissue a book or record is to publish or release it a second time.

clue.text: Hospital preparation military engineers paid to go without

indicators.note: 'without' in its old sense means outside, so one part sits outside the other

blocks.note: PD is the abbreviation for paid
Royal Electrical and Mechanical Engineers, a British Army corps

explanation.surface: Army engineers given money so they can do without hospital treatment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without' looks like 'lacking', but here it keeps its old meaning of outside. Military engineers are usually RE in crosswords; this time it is the longer corps abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: Premed is short for premedication, the sedative drugs given to a patient before surgery.

clue.text: Trailblazer on expedition initially requiring external support?

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so only a word's first letter is used
needing something on the outside means being wrapped by it

blocks.note: taken as written
the first letter of expedition
a pier is a supporting pillar or column

explanation.surface: An explorer on a journey who needs help from outside to begin with.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark admits that 'external support' is a playful way to say the support goes on the outside of the other letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A pioneer is the first to explore or settle new ground, opening a path for others.

clue.text: Senior citizen flaying member of fighting force

indicators.note: flaying strips off the skin, so the outer letters are removed

blocks.note: a soldier serves in an army

explanation.surface: An elderly person thrashing a serviceman.
explanation.walkthrough: SOLDIER with its first and last letters peeled off.
explanation.definitionFit: Oldie is a colloquial word for an elderly person, a pensioner in informal speech.

clue.text: Famous actor originally involved in musical

indicators.note: originally means at the start, so only the first letter is kept
being in something means sitting inside it

blocks.note: the first letter of involved
Oliver!, Lionel Bart's stage musical

explanation.surface: A well-known actor who started out in a stage musical.
explanation.walkthrough: I goes into OLIVER. Laurence Olivier was the great English stage and film actor.
explanation.definitionFit: Laurence Olivier was among the most celebrated Shakespearean performers of the twentieth century.

clue.text: Pigment made from mineral aggregate surrounding church

indicators.note: to surround is to enclose on all sides

blocks.note: ore is rock containing metal or minerals
CH is the abbreviation for church

explanation.surface: An artist's colour produced from crushed rock dug up around a church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Made from' is a link: the pigment is produced from the wordplay, which also hints at how ochre is really dug from the earth.
explanation.definitionFit: Ochre is an earthy yellow-brown clay used since prehistoric times as a colouring for paint.

clue.text: Most of rite mother used to somehow endure to the end

indicators.note: most of something is all but a little, so the final letter goes
done somehow means done in some unspecified way, so the letters can be in any order

blocks.note: rite without its last letter
taken as written

explanation.surface: A ritual Mum once followed, which she somehow kept going to the finish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Used to' looks like a past-habit phrase, but its six letters are fodder along with RIT and MOTHER.
explanation.definitionFit: To ride out a storm is to survive a crisis without giving in, persisting until it is over.

clue.text: Tin containing damsons primarily in very small country

indicators.note: primarily means first of all, so the opening letter is taken
being in something means sitting inside it
to contain is to hold inside

blocks.note: Sn is the chemical symbol for tin
wee is Scottish for little
the first letter of damsons

explanation.surface: A can of damsons in a tiny state.
explanation.walkthrough: D goes into WEE, and that goes into SN. 'Very small country' wants to be the definition; only 'country' is.
explanation.definitionFit: Sweden is a Scandinavian nation, so it is a straightforward example of a sovereign state.

clue.text: Tear about always, being vicar, perhaps

indicators.note: about means around, so one part surrounds the other

blocks.note: to rend is to rip
ever means at all times

explanation.surface: Rushing around all the time, as a busy clergyman does.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tear about' reads as dashing to and fro, but 'tear' means rip and 'about' is the wrapping signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A vicar is one example of an ordained cleric, the title given to members of the clergy; 'perhaps' flags it as an instance.
